facts.statement: The genus Birkenia was described by Traquair in 1898.
Three species are known within the genus: B. campbelli, B. elegans, and B. robusta.
facts.quote: subdivision: B. campbelli Traquair, 1898 B. elegans Traquair, 1898 B. robusta Blom, Märss and Miller, 2002

facts.statement: Birkenia lived during the Middle Silurian in Northern Europe and possibly the Earliest Devonian in Arctic Canada.
facts.quote: Birkenia is a genus of extinct anaspid fish from Middle Silurian strata of Northern Europe, and Middle Silurian to possibly Earliest Devonian strata of Arctic Canada.

facts.statement: These fish had small plates covering their heads and rod-shaped scales arranged in a chevron pattern on their trunks.
facts.quote: Birkeniid anaspids are covered by a series of small plates on the head and rod-shaped scales in a cheveron-like pattern on the trunk.

facts.statement: Intact fossils of B. elegans indicate the animal grew up to 10.0 cm long and was an active swimmer.
facts.quote: Intact fossil specimens of B. elegans suggest the living animal reached a length of up to 10.0 cm, and was an active swimmer.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows a modified rib structure that is narrow at the ends and broadens toward the middle to form a raised, slightly angled ridge.
facts.quote: Fossil specimens also show a rib that is modified by being narrow at the ends and gradually broadens and rises towards the middle of the scale, where a major elevation is developed that is expressed as a raised and slightly angled ridge.

facts.statement: Birkenia existed between 443.1 and 422.7 million years ago during the Rhuddanian to Ludfordian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Rhuddanian to Ludfordian (443.1 to 422.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: Birkenia belongs to the family Birkeniidae.
Birkenia is classified within the class Anaspida.
